label: Lattices and Minkowski's Theorem
notes: This chapter, printed pages seventeen through twenty-eight, opens discrete geometry's bridge to number theory. We meet lattices as integer spans of a basis, measure them by their determinant, and prove Minkowski's theorem: a large symmetric convex body must swallow a nonzero lattice point.

label: What Is a Lattice
notes: A lattice is the set of all integer combinations of a fixed basis of independent vectors. It is a discrete subgroup of Euclidean space, infinite yet evenly spaced. The integer grid is the simplest example, but skewed bases give richer tilings that we will measure carefully.

label: Fundamental Parallelepiped
notes: Each lattice carves space into translated copies of one fundamental parallelepiped spanned by the basis. Its volume, the determinant, equals the absolute value of the basis matrix determinant. Different bases give the same lattice, and crucially the same determinant, so covolume is a genuine lattice invariant.

label: The Determinant Is Invariant
notes: Two bases generate the same lattice exactly when a unimodular integer matrix relates them. Such matrices have determinant plus or minus one, so the covolume is unchanged. This invariance lets us speak of the lattice determinant without referencing any particular basis we happened to choose.

label: Minkowski's Theorem
notes: Minkowski's theorem is the chapter's centerpiece. If a convex body is symmetric about the origin and its volume exceeds two to the dimension times the lattice determinant, it must contain a nonzero lattice point. Convexity and symmetry are both essential; dropping either breaks the conclusion immediately.

label: Proof by Folding mod 2L
notes: Scale the body by one half and fold it onto the torus modulo two times the lattice. The folded volume exceeds the cell, so by pigeonhole two distinct points collide. Their difference is a nonzero lattice point, and symmetry plus convexity place it inside the original body.

label: Blichfeldt and Generality
notes: Blichfeldt's lemma underlies the folding step: any set of volume exceeding the determinant has two points differing by a lattice vector. Minkowski's theorem follows for arbitrary lattices, not just the integer grid, because we may transform any lattice to the standard one by a linear map.

label: Successive Minima
notes: The successive minima record the smallest dilations at which a symmetric body captures one, two, up through d independent lattice directions. Minkowski's second theorem bounds their product against the determinant, refining the first theorem from a single short vector to a whole independent system.

label: Sums of Two Squares
notes: A classic payoff: every prime congruent to one modulo four is a sum of two squares. Build a lattice from a square root of minus one modulo the prime, apply Minkowski to a disk, and the captured lattice point furnishes exactly the two integers whose squares sum to the prime.

label: Diophantine Approximation
notes: Minkowski's theorem proves simultaneous Diophantine approximation: any reals admit integer numerators sharing one denominator that approximate them all well. The proof picks a thin symmetric box of the right volume, and the guaranteed nonzero lattice point inside it encodes the simultaneous rational approximation we wanted.

label: Short Vectors and Hardness
notes: Minkowski guarantees a lattice vector no longer than a determinant-based bound, but finding the shortest vector is computationally hard in high dimension. This gap between existence and algorithm powers lattice-based cryptography, where short-vector difficulty secures schemes believed safe even against quantum adversaries.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We defined lattices, measured them by the invariant determinant, proved Minkowski's theorem by folding modulo two times the lattice, and harvested number-theoretic fruit. The themes of covolume, convex symmetry, and pigeonhole recur throughout discrete geometry and feed directly into later counting and packing chapters.
